challenges.title: Hidden in plain sight
challenges.objective: Find the file in your home directory that holds the flag, and read it.
challenges.briefing:
Two files were written into your home directory before you started.

Both have names that begin with a dot. A plain listing leaves those out,
which is why a directory can look emptier than it is.

One of the two holds your flag. The other is noise.

Your home directory is /tmp/gen4.
hints:
A listing command usually has a flag of its own for showing everything.
Try the short one with -a, or the long one with -A.

Dot files are ordinary files. Once you can see them, read them the same
way you would read anything else. One of them has a line beginning 'flag:'.

challenges.title: Owner only
challenges.objective: Read the file that only your account is allowed to open.
challenges.briefing:
Every file carries a permission string, and a long listing prints it in
the first column. Nine characters, in three groups of three:

    rwx   rwx   rwx
    you   group other

A dash means that permission is not granted. So -rw-r--r-- is readable by
everyone, and -rw------- is readable by you alone.

Three files were written into your home directory. One of them is yours
alone. Find it and read it.
hints:
A long listing shows the permissions for every file at once. That is the
long flag with a lower case L, not a one.

Look for the file whose group and other permissions are all dashes. The
name of that file starts with the word private.

challenges.title: Two halves
challenges.objective: Join the two halves of the flag, which sit in different directories.
challenges.briefing:
A flag was split down the middle. The first half is in one file, the
second half is in another, and they are not in the same directory.

The awkward part is that each half is on its own line. Put them together
and you get a line break in the middle of the flag, which is not what you
want.

Two commands are worth knowing here. Listing a tree shows you what is
under a directory without walking into each one by hand. And tr can
delete characters, including the newline character, if you name it.

Everything is under your home directory. Start there.
hints:
There is a command whose whole job is showing you a directory tree.
Once you have it, you can see both halves at once.

Concatenate the two files with cat, then remove the line break with tr.
The name for a newline inside quotes is a backslash followed by a lower
case n.

challenges.title: Read the log
challenges.objective: Find the flag in a web server log, without reading every line.
challenges.briefing:
A web server log holds one line per request. Four fields, in order: the
address that asked, the time, the request itself, and the status code.

    address - - [time] "GET /path HTTP/1.1" status size

There are dozens of lines, and reading them by hand is a waste of your
time. A search tool will find a pattern in a file and show you only the
lines that match.

One warning. More than one line contains something that looks like a
flag. Only one of them is real, and you can tell them apart by shape:
your flag holds exactly sixteen characters, and every one of them is a
digit or a letter from a to f.
hints:
Search the file rather than opening it. The tool you want is grep, and
the option that prints only the matching part of a line is -o.

Use a pattern rather than a plain word, so the decoy cannot match. A
character class of the sixteen hex digits, repeated sixteen times, is
enough to describe the real flag and nothing else.

challenges.title: Twice over
challenges.objective: Undo two layers of encoding to get the flag back.
challenges.briefing:
Encoding is not encryption. Encryption needs a key, and without the key
there is nothing to do. Encoding is just a different way of writing the
same thing, and anyone who knows the scheme can reverse it.

Two schemes were used here, one after the other.

The first turns three bytes into four printable characters, so that
binary data can travel through systems that only carry text. You can spot
it by the alphabet it uses: capitals, lower case, digits, and often one or
two equals signs at the end as padding.

The second is older and simpler. It shifts every letter thirteen places
along the alphabet, wrapping around at the end. Because there are
twenty-six letters, running it again undoes it.

Undo them in the reverse order to the one they were applied in.
hints:
The payload is the last line of the file, and it is the first scheme.
The tool that decodes it is the same one that encoded it, with -d.

After decoding you will have readable text with the letters shifted.
Shift them back with tr, mapping the upper and lower case alphabets onto
themselves rotated by thirteen. The rotation is its own inverse, so the
same command both applies and removes it.

challenges.title: Inside the archive
challenges.objective: Read a file out of a compressed backup without unpacking it.
challenges.briefing:
A backup was taken of a directory and stored as a single compressed file.
It sits under a backups directory in your home.

You could unpack the whole thing, but that scatters files everywhere and
you only want one of them. The archiving tool can list what is inside
without extracting anything, and it can print a single member straight to
your terminal.

Two options do that. One lists, one writes to standard output, which is
the same thing as printing it.
hints:
Ask the archive what it holds before you touch it. The tar option for
listing is -t, and for a gzipped archive you also need -z and -f.

Once you know the member's name, ask tar to write it to standard output
with -O, alongside -x for extract and -z for gzip.
